summary: Operational plumbing for the API. A thread-safe `Metrics` registry tracks request counts, error rate, latency percentiles, per-route stats and events ingested per minute; a pure-ASGI `RequestContextMiddleware` tags every response with `X-Request-ID`/`X-Response-Time`, writes the access log and feeds `Metrics`; and `RateLimiter` is a per-client token bucket. `iip/app.py` installs the middleware, `iip/routes/deps.py` turns the limiter into a dependency, and `/api/v1/integration/metrics` in `iip/routes/system.py` serves `metrics.snapshot()` to the Integration page.

notes.text: Module docstring summary: request IDs, access logs, latency and throughput metrics, and rate limiting all live here.

Explains why: these are the SLIs (service level indicators) an integration team watches: how many calls a client makes, how fast the API answers as p50/p95/p99 percentiles, how many calls fail, and how many events flow per minute.
Postpones evaluation of type hints, so annotations such as `deque[float]` are never evaluated at import time.
`logging` writes the access log; `re` checks incoming request ids.
`threading` provides the locks that protect shared counters; `time` provides the wall-clock, high-resolution and monotonic clocks.
`uuid` generates request ids; `Counter` (a dict that counts) and `deque` (a list with an optional maximum length) hold the metrics.
`MutableHeaders` lets the middleware edit the headers of an outgoing ASGI response message in place.

Type names from the ASGI spec: an app is a callable taking `scope` (information about the request), `receive` (reads incoming messages) and `send` (emits outgoing messages); a `Message` is one such message, a plain dict.
Named logger for the access log, so its lines are labelled `iip.http`.
The shape of a request id the middleware will echo back: 1 to 64 letters, digits, dots, underscores or dashes.
`Metrics` is the in-memory registry behind everything the Integration page charts.
`window=2000` sets how many recent latency samples are kept for the percentiles.

One lock guards every field, because several threads use the registry: the middleware records requests on the event loop thread, while sync endpoints and the traffic generator call it from worker threads.
Wall-clock start time, used to compute uptime.
Total requests, and total server errors (5xx), since start-up.
Counts responses by status class: `2xx`, `4xx`, `5xx`.
Per-route statistics keyed by `"METHOD /route"`: call count, error count and summed milliseconds.
A rolling window: `deque(maxlen=window)` automatically discards the oldest value once 2,000 are stored, which bounds memory and keeps the percentiles about recent traffic.
Events ingested per epoch minute (whole minutes since 1 January 1970), the raw data behind the throughput chart.
`observe` records one finished HTTP request: method, templated route, status code and duration in milliseconds.
Takes the lock so concurrent updates cannot interleave and lose counts.
Counts the request.
Adds the boolean `status >= 500` to the error total. Python booleans are integers (`True == 1`), so only server errors increase it.
Integer division turns a status code into its class, for example 404 becomes `"4xx"`.
Stores the latency sample in the rolling window.
Fetches this route's stats dict, creating a zeroed one on first use (`setdefault`).
Updates the route's counters. Note the per-route `errors` counts every status `>= 400` (client mistakes included), unlike the global counter, which counts only 5xx.
`record_ingest` counts events entering the pipeline; the events route, the simulation route and the live-traffic generator call it.
The current epoch minute: seconds since 1970 divided by 60, rounded down.
Under the lock, adds `count` to this minute's bucket.
Deletes buckets older than an hour so memory stays bounded. The list comprehension collects the old keys first, because deleting from a dict while iterating over it directly raises an error.
`snapshot` returns the JSON-ready summary served by `/integration/metrics`.
Holds the lock only long enough to copy the data out.
A sorted copy of the latency window, needed to read percentiles by position.
One summary per route, with average latency (total milliseconds divided by calls) rounded to two decimals.
The last 30 minutes of ingest counts, oldest first (`k` runs from 29 down to 0); minutes without events read as 0.
Copies the plain counters into local variables so the remaining work can happen after the lock is released.

`pct` returns a percentile by **nearest rank**: take the sorted samples and pick the value at position `p * n`, clamped to the last index. p50 is the median, while p95 and p99 describe the slowest 5% and 1% of requests, the tail an average hides; with no samples it returns 0.
Builds the snapshot dictionary, outside the lock.
Seconds since the registry was created, which in practice is process uptime.
Total requests and total server errors.
Errors as a fraction of requests (0.0123 means 1.23%), guarded against division by zero.
The status-class breakdown copied earlier.
Latency percentiles and the average, in milliseconds, all from the same sorted window.
The 30-value ingest series for the throughput chart.
The 12 busiest routes, sorted by call count descending; the closing brace ends the snapshot dict.
The process-wide registry, shared by the middleware, the routes and the live-traffic generator.
`RequestContextMiddleware` wraps the whole application, so it sees every request first and every response last.

Docstring: tag every response with `X-Request-ID` and `X-Response-Time`, log one line per API call and feed `Metrics`. It is **pure ASGI** rather than Starlette's `BaseHTTPMiddleware`, which re-routes every response body through its own internal stream; wrapping `send` directly lets the long-lived SSE stream pass straight through, chunk by chunk.
Starlette constructs the middleware with the inner `app` it wraps; `registry` defaults to the shared `metrics` but a fresh `Metrics` could be passed in, for example in a test.
Stores the wrapped app and the metrics registry.
The ASGI entry point, called once per connection with `scope`, `receive` and `send`.
Anything that is not an HTTP request (such as the `lifespan` startup and shutdown messages) is passed straight through untouched.

Reads the caller's `X-Request-ID` header, if any. ASGI headers are a list of lowercase byte-string pairs, hence `b"x-request-id"`. Latin-1 can decode any byte sequence, so an odd header can no longer crash the request with a decoding error.

Reuses the caller's id when it is a safe token (see `_SAFE_ID`), so one request can be traced across systems; otherwise it creates a short random id from a UUID. Echoing arbitrary text used to fail with an encoding error, a 500, for characters such as `€`.
`perf_counter` is a high-resolution clock meant for measuring durations.
Assumes 500 until a response actually starts, so a request whose handler crashes before sending anything is still recorded as a server error.
A wrapper around `send`: every message the app sends passes through it on its way to the server.
`nonlocal` lets this inner function update the outer `status` variable.
The `http.response.start` message carries the status code and headers (body chunks follow later), so this is where the status is captured.
Wraps the message's header list so headers can be added to it in place.
Echoes the request id back, so a client can quote it when reporting a problem.
Time from request arrival to the moment headers are sent, formatted like `12.3ms`. For a streamed response that is time to first byte, not total duration.
Forwards the (possibly modified) message to the real server.
Runs the rest of the application with the wrapped `send`.
`finally` runs whether the app returned normally or raised, so failed requests are measured too.
The request path, for example `/api/v1/users/USR-1001`.
Only API calls are measured: static files and the dashboard page are skipped, and so is the SSE `/stream`, whose connection can stay open for hours and would wreck the latency figures.
Total elapsed milliseconds.

The route template the router matched, such as `/users/{user_id}`: FastAPI leaves the matched route in `scope`. Paths that matched nothing share one `(unmatched)` entry; keying by the raw path used to add a permanent entry for every distinct unknown URL.
Records the request in `Metrics`.
One access-log line per call: method, path, status, duration and request id. The `%s` placeholders let `logging` build the message only if the line is actually emitted.
`RateLimiter` implements the **token bucket** algorithm, with one bucket per client.
Docstring: `per_minute` requests a minute on average, with bursts of up to `per_minute` requests allowed.
Takes the allowed requests per minute (`IIP_RATE_LIMIT_PER_MINUTE`, 240 by default).
Bucket capacity, the largest burst a client can make; `max(..., 1)` guarantees at least one token.
Refill speed in tokens per second, so an empty bucket refills completely in exactly one minute.
Maps each client key to `(tokens left, time of last update)`. Idle entries are pruned in `hit`, so the map can't grow without bound.
A lock, because sync dependencies run in FastAPI's thread pool and two requests could update the same bucket at the same time.
`hit` is called by the `rate_limit` dependency once for every throttled request (the write endpoints and `/ai/ask`).
Docstring: returns 0 when the request is allowed, otherwise the number of seconds until a token becomes available.
`time.monotonic()` never jumps backwards (the wall clock can, when the system time is changed), which makes it safe for measuring elapsed time.
The read-modify-write of the bucket happens under the lock.

Prunes idle clients once more than 10,000 buckets exist. A bucket untouched for a minute has refilled completely, so forgetting it changes nothing for that client, and memory stays bounded however many addresses call the API.
Loads this client's bucket; a first-time client starts with a full bucket.
Lazy refill: adds the tokens earned since the last update (elapsed seconds times the refill rate), capped at capacity. No background timer is needed.
At least one whole token: spend it, save the new state and return `0.0`, meaning allowed.
Not enough tokens: saves the refilled state and returns how long until the bucket holds one token, `(1 - tokens) / refill_per_second` seconds. `deps.py` sends this back in a `Retry-After` header.
